DEPARTMENT W LAW AND MOTION RULINGS


Case Number: 22VECV02293    Hearing Date: June 25, 2026    Dept: W

Hearing Date: 

Thursday, June 25, 20256 

Case Name: 

Darra Hall v. The Hartford Life and Accident Insurance Company 

Case No.: 

22VECV02293 

MOTION 

Default Prove Up 

Moving Party: 

Defendants and Interpleader Plaintiffs Protective Life Insurance Company (“Protective”) and West Coast Life Insurance Company 

Responding Party: 

None. 

Notice:  

Proof of Service on April 29, 2026. 

Filings: 

Request for Entry of Default Judgment – 4/30/26 

Declaration of Charles Chineduh in Support – 4/30/26 

Summary of the Case – 4/30/26 

Proposed Judgment – 4/30/26 

 

Holding: 

 

The Court TENTATIVELY GRANTS Defendant’s Request for Default Judgment. 

 

Background: 

 

This case is about the rightful beneficiary of two life insurance policies. The ownership of both of these policies has already been adjudicated. As a brief recap, on May 17, 2007, non-party Patsy Hall applied for a $4,000,000 life insurance policy from Defendant West Coast Life Insurance Company. The policy was issued to the Patsy Hall Irrevocable Life Trust, who eventually transferred it to CSSEL GBT, a Credit Suisse subsidiary. CSSEL brought a motion for summary judgment as to the ownership of this policy. The Court ruled in favor of CSSEL on January 22, 2026. 

 

Ownership of the second policy was the subject of a recent Motion for Summary Judgment. On December 13, 2007, non-party Patsy Hall applied for a second, $2,500,000 life insurance policy from Protective Life Insurance Company. The original beneficiary of this policy was the Patsy Hall Irrevocable Life Trust. On September 19, 2012, the rights of this policy were transferred to PF Participation Funding Trust. On April 16, 2026, this Court granted PF Participation Funding Trust’s Motion for Summary Judgment. Thus, the determination of the rightful beneficiaries of these policies has been fully adjudicated. 

 

The instant default prove-up is brought by Moving Defendants/Interpleader Plaintiffs West Coast Life Ins. Co and Protective Life Insurance Company (herein, “Interpleader Plaintiffs”). Interpleader Plaintiffs are the insurers who sold the disputed policies and are responsible for paying out the proceeds of Patsy Hall’s policies. 

 

On May 6, 2025, Interpleader Plaintiffs filed both their Answer to the original lawsuit, and filed a Cross-Complaint against both Darra Hall, and every other Defendant in the case. Their Crossclaim brought only a single request – to deposit the disputed policy proceeds into the registry of the Court. Essentially, Interpleader Plaintiffs agree that these policies need to be paid out, but the dispute over who is the rightful recipient means they cannot disburse the funds. Moreover, Interpleader Plaintiffs have no stake in who wins this case. So rather than be dragged into this dispute, Interpleader Plaintiffs wish to deposit the money into an interest-bearing account that the Court can distribute from once the case resolves. 

 

Christopher Hall, the trustee of the Patsy Hall Irrevocable Life Trust, never responded to this Cross-Complaint. Interpleader Plaintiffs submitted their initial request for entry of default judgment on July 14, 2025. Default was entered against Defendant Christopher Hall, but Interpleader Plaintiffs never moved forward. 

 

On April 30, 2026, Interpleader Plaintiffs once again submitted a request for entry of default against Defendant Christopher Hall. 

 

On May 1, 2026, Interpleader Plaintiffs failed to appear for their default prove-up hearing. The Court scheduled an OSC Re: Failure to Appear. 

 

Now, the Court once again hears the default prove-up hearing, alongside an OSC Re: Failure to Appear. 

 

Analysis: 

 

CCP § 585 permits entry of a judgment after a Defendant has failed to timely answer after being properly served. A party seeking judgment on the default by the Court must file a Request for Court Judgment, and: (1) a brief summary of the case; (2) declarations or other admissible evidence in support of the judgment requested; (3) interest computations as necessary; (4) a memorandum of costs and disbursements; (5) a proposed form of judgment; (6) a dismissal of all parties against whom judgment is not sought; (7) a dismissal of all parties against whom judgment is not sought or an application for separate judgment under CCP § 579, supported by a showing of grounds for each judgment; (8) exhibits as necessary; and (9) a request for attorneys’ fees if allowed by statute or by the agreement of the parties. (CRC Rule 3.1800.)¿ 

 

  1. Use of JC Form CIV-100  

 

Yes – see Request for Entry of Default Judgment.  

¿ 

  1. Dismissal or judgment of non-parties to the judgment 

 

Yes – Through two recent MSJs, this Court has determined that CSSEL is the rightful beneficiary of the first life insurance policy, and that PF Participation Funding Trust is the rightful beneficiary of the second policy. 

 

  1. Declaration of non-military status for each defendant 

 

Yes. See Charles Chineduh Declaration, Paragraph 9. 

 

  1. Summary of the case 

 

Yes. See Summary of the Case, filed April 30, 2026. 

 

  1. 585(d) declarations/admissible evidence in support 

 

Yes. See Charles Chineduh Declaration. 

 

  1. Exhibits (as necessary)¿ 

 

No exhibits necessary. 

 

  1. Interest computation (as necessary)  

 

No monetary award requested. 

¿ 

  1. Cost memorandum  

 

No request for costs. 

¿ 

  1. Request for attorney fees (Local Rule 3.214)  

 

No request for attorney fees. 
 ¿ 

  1. Proposed form of judgment 

 

It is somewhat unclear what judgment Interpleader Plaintiffs seek, as their CIV-100 form does not include a request for either monetary or non-monetary relief. However, in the Declaration of Mr. Chineduh, Interpleader Plaintiffs do request, “default judgment in favor of Interpleader Plaintiffs and against Christopher Hall is proper with regard to the Interpleader Complaint.” (Chineduh Decl. ¶ 10.) 

 

Based on Interpleader Plaintiffs’ original cross-complaint, they request the following relief: 

 

First, that the disputed policy proceeds are deposited into an interest-bearing account with the Registry of the Court. (Cross-Complaint p. 8:10-12.)  

 

Second, that the Court, “adjudicate the issue of which of the Interpleader Defendants are rightfully entitled to the Policies’ Proceeds.” (Id. p. 8:4-5.) 

 

Third, that “the Court enter an order enjoining each of the Interpleader Defendants, their agents, attorneys, and/or assigns, from instituting or maintaining any action in any court or forum against the Interpleader Plaintiffs.” (Id. p. 8:6-8.) 

 

Fourth, “[t]hat an award be made to the Interpleader Plaintiffs out of the funds to be deposited into the Registry of the Court, as reimbursement for the costs, attorneys’ fees, and other expenses the Interpleader Plaintiffs are compelled to expend in the prosecution of this lawsuit.” (Id. p. 8:10-12.) 

 

Fifth, that, “the Interpleader Plaintiffs be dismissed with prejudice from this action and discharged from any and all further liability with respect to, affecting, or in any way arising out of the Policies with an express finding of finality.” (Id. p. 8:13-15.) 

 

Given these requests, the Court believes it can grant partial relief.  

 

First, the Court takes no issue with having the policy proceeds deposited into an interest-bearing account with the Registry of the Court. 

 

Second, the Court has already determined the rightful beneficiaries in this case. 

 

Third, because this motion is only brought with respect to Defendant Christopher Hall in his role as trustee, the Court could only enjoin Christopher Hall as trustee from bringing further suit. 

 

Fourth, the Court cannot grant the request for costs and attorney fees, as Interpleader Plaintiffs provide no basis for their reasonable costs or fees. (See Request for Entry of Default; see also Chineduh Decl.) 

 

Fifth, the Court can dismiss Plaintiffs from this case. 

 

For these reasons, the Court TENTATIVELY GRANTS Defendant’s Request for Default Judgment, as set forth herein. 

 

Conclusion:  

 

The Court TENTATIVELY GRANTS Defendant’s Request for Default Judgment, as set forth herein.

Case Number: 25VECV06370    Hearing Date: June 25, 2026    Dept: W

Hearing Date:

Thursday, June 25, 2026

Case Name:

Great American Insurance Company v. Ridge Productions, Inc., et al.

Case No.:

25VECV06370

MOTIONS

Motion to Preclude Evidence at Trial

Moving Party:

Defendant Ridge Productions, Inc.

Responding Party:

Plaintiff Great American Insurance Company

Notice:

Proof of Service on February 19, 2026.

Documents:

Demand for Bill of Particulars – 1/26/26

Defendant’s Motion to Preclude Evidence at Trial – 2/29/26

Plaintiff’s Opposition – 4/3/26

Moving Defendant’s Reply – 4/6/26

Minute Order – 4/23/26

Defendant’s Supplemental Reply – 6/4/26

Plaintiff’s Supplemental Opposition

 

Ruling:

 

The Court DENIES Defendant’s Motion to Preclude Evidence at Trial Re: Plaintiff’s causes of action for open book account and account stated.

 

Relevant Background:

 

This is an open book accounts case. Plaintiff is Great American Insurance Company. Defendant is Ridge Productions, Inc. Plaintiff alleges that Defendant is $55,547.84 in debt to them. Plaintiff provides no other details!

 

On November 6, 2025, Plaintiff brought suit against Defendant alleging three causes of action: 1) open book account, 2) account stated, and 3) reasonable value.

 

On February 19, 2026, Defendant moved to preclude Plaintiff from introducing evidence of these accounts at trial.

 

On April 23, 2026, this Court continued this motion, as Plaintiff failed to attach a detailed copy of the request bill of particulars.

 

Now, the Court once again hears this motion.

 

Analysis:

 

Defendant moves to preclude Plaintiff from introducing evidence of the account that forms the basis of this action. (Mot. to Preclude, p. 3:21-22.)

 

Defendant brings this motion under CCP § 454 which states that, “[i]t is not necessary for a party to set forth in a pleading the items of an account therein alleged, but he must deliver to the adverse party, within ten days after a demand thereof in writing, a copy of the account, or be precluded from giving evidence thereof. The court or judge thereof may order a further account when the one delivered is too general, or is defective in any particular.” (CCP § 454.)

 

Here, Defendant served Plaintiff with a Demand for Bill of Particulars on January 26, 2026. (See generally, Demand for Particulars.) Per CCP § 454, Plaintiff had until February 5, 2026, to produce a bill of particulars detailing the account that this lawsuit is based on. (Brenner Decl. ¶ 3.) Plaintiff did not submit a response by February 5, 2026. (Id. ¶ 5.) Instead, on February 9, 2025, Plaintiff’s counsel produced a written summary of what the account kinda-sorta entailed. (Mot. to Preclude, Ex. 2.) This document contained no specifics numbers related to the account at issue in this case. (Ibid.)

 

Under California case law, this production is insufficient. The purpose of this code section is, "to give the adverse party reasonable notice of the items constituting the claim which he is required to meet, so that he may prepare for trial." (Gilmore v. Hill (1957) 152 Cal.App.2d 881, 882-883 [quoting Ames v. Bell (1907) 5 Cal.App. 1, 4].) For an example of how to analyze this motion, the Court looks to the case of Banchero v. Coffis. There, a plaintiff submitted a statement similar the one in the case at hand which merely summarized four types of alleged services that were given. (Banchero v. Coffis (1950) 96 Cal.App.2d 717, 718.) Defendant brought a motion to preclude evidence under CCP § 454, but the trial court denied the motion. (Ibid.) On appeal, this ruling was overturned. The court of appeals stated that the denial of the motion to preclude was improper, because the bill of accounts Plaintiff produced was insufficient. The court explained that, "[a] proper bill would have at least shown how much was claimed for each one of the four services alleged." (Id. at 722.) The court went on to explain that, “[w]ithout an exposition of plaintiff's position by a bill of particulars the estate in the case at bar could not adequately prepare its defense on this important phase of the case. Hence, in short, it was denied a fair trial.” (Id. at 724.) This case shows that California courts take CCP § 454 at its word. Thus, courts should preclude evidence of an account when a plaintiff fails to submit a timely copy of the account.

 

In their original Opposition, Plaintiff insisted that preclusion is not the only remedy. (Opp. p. 1-2.) Instead, Plaintiff points to the language of CCP § 454, which states that, “[t]he court or judge thereof may order a further account when the one delivered is too general, or is defective in any particular.” (CCP § 454.)

 

While Plaintiff cited no case law in their Opposition, the Court agreed that a plain reading of the statute allowed it leeway to order a further account, when a previous submission is too general. In this case, Plaintiff’s submission was untimely and too general. (Mot. to Preclude, Ex. 2.) Thus, this Court ordered Plaintiff to produce a further account. Specifically, the Court ordered Plaintiff to produce a detailed copy of the account at issue no later than May 26, 2026. (Minute Order, 4/23/26.) Plaintiff complied with this order.

 

On April 23, 2026, just minutes after the Court’s previous hearing on this motion, Plaintiff served on Defendant another copy of their bill of particulars. (Supp. Reply, Brenner Decl. ¶ 4; see also, Supp. Reply, Ex. B, Ex. 1.) The first three pages of this new submission are identical to the original bill of particulars this Court found inadequate. (See Supp. Reply, Ex. A; see also, Supp. Reply, Ex. B.) The second two pages, a.k.a. Exhibit 1, are labeled “Statement of Account”. (Supp. Reply, Ex. B.) Here, Plaintiff provides a short list of accounts and numbers, which appear to be premium totals and dates of payment receipts. (Ibid.)

 

In their Supplemental Opposition, Defendant argues that Plaintiff’s newest production is insufficient, because it is not detailed enough. Specifically, Defendant asserts that, “Plaintiff generally describes insurance policies, generally describes premium charges, generally describes audits, and generally describes how premiums are determined. None of which constitutes an account. The document contains no ledger. It contains no statement of debits and credits. It contains no payroll records. It contains no audit worksheets. It contains no classification calculations. It contains no transaction history. It contains no records from which the claimed balance may be independently determined.” (Supplemental Reply, p. 5:8-15.) Defendant asserts that these lack of details are fatal.

 

In support of the assertion that these details matter, Defendant cites to CCP § 337a, which states that, “[t]he term ‘book account’ means a detailed statement which constitutes the principal record of one or more transactions between a debtor and a creditor arising out of a contract or some fiduciary relation, and shows the debits and credits in connection therewith, and against whom and in favor of whom entries are made, is entered in the regular course of business . . . and is kept in a reasonably permanent form and manner. . .” (CCP § 337a(a).)

 

The Court finds that Plaintiff’s supplemental bill of particulars is sufficient to satisfy CCP § 454 and CCP § 337a(a). Plaintiff has provided a document with the alleged outstanding premiums for multiple workers compensation policies, as well as the dates and amounts of payment received by Plaintiff. (Supp. Reply, Ex. B, Ex. 1.) That is precisely what CCP § 337a(a) asks for.

 

Moreover, as explained above, the purpose of a bill of particulars is to furnish a defendant with the details of the items charged and to amplify the complaint so that the defendant may intelligently prepare a defense. (Meredith v. Marks (1963) 212 Cal.App.2d 265, 269.) While these numbers do not amount to a total and exhaustive copy record of all the payroll records, debits and credits, and transaction history between the parties, they do clearly indicate the amounts Plaintiff has alleged, the accounts these claims are connected to, and the payments made by Defendant towards these accounts. Thus, Plaintiff has sufficient information to understand the allegations made against them and may intelligently prepare a defense to these claims. 

For these reasons, the Court is satisfied with Plaintiff’s production, and DENIES Defendant’s motion to preclude evidence at trial. 

Conclusion: 

The Court DENIES Defendant’s Motion to Preclude Evidence at Trial Re: Plaintiff’s causes of action for open book account and account stated.
